utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. While we are waiting for the witness to come in, the Chamber would mention that on the 25th of March the Defence applied for the amendment of two documents admitted as Defence Exhibits D636 and D703 which had been uploaded incorrectly in e-court. Now leave to amend the exhibits is granted. Exhibit D636 shall be identified as document D011-1858 for the B/C/S version and D010-4417 for the English translation. Page 3 of the English translation of Exhibit D703 shall be removed from the e-court as it was erroneously uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation which is shown to you. Read it aloud. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, before we begin your testimony today, I'm going to ask you, first of all, to pause a little bit after you hear the question since we are both speaking the same language. So make a pause and then begin your answer because in that way we will make it possible for the interpreters to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Milan Cankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of March, 1948, in the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and if yes, from what date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs from 1976 until the 31st of December, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And on the 31st of December, 2002, did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I retired on the 1st of January, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you briefly explain to us what your duties were in the Ministry of Internal Affairs during your period of work there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1976 and then until 1978, I was working on the exploitation of the communication system in the MUP. From 1978 until 1981 I worked as a course leader and lecturer at the high school for Internal Affairs education, and I dealt with communications courses from 1981 until 1993 or 1994, I don't know exactly. I worked on monitoring measuring systems in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. All of this was in the communications administration. From 1994, I think, I was transferred to the police administration where I worked on procurement of communications equipment, and vehicles. Also different parts for vehicles. I worked on these assignments in the police administration until 2001 when the gendarmerie was formed, and this is where I was the chief of the communications department. I stayed there until I retired, until the 31st of December, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. I'm just going to put one question to you for the purposes of the transcript, since in a few places in the transcript it said you worked in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Were you working in the Ministry of Internal Affairs or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: All of the posts I held were in the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia. I never worked in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. You told us briefly which jobs you worked on, so to summarise, I would put this question to you: All of the duties you performed during your professional career, did they all have to do with communications?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the duties in the Ministry of Internal Affairs that I had had to do exclusively with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us something about your education?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm an electrical engineer. Engineer of telecommunications by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cankovic, I'm going to ask you to specify for us exactly which duties you carried out in the Ministry of Internal Affairs in 1998 and 1999 until the time that the NATO bombing ended.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I was a member of the staff in Kosovo and Metohija which had its seat in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to see Exhibit P760 on our monitors, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document to be shown, Mr. Cankovic, can you please tell us when in 1998 did you become a member of the staff, and exactly which staff was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed a member of the staff on the 11th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you to look at the document that we can see on the screen. This is a decision on the composition of the staff leaders and members of the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for the Autonomous Province for Kosovo and Metohija, and I'm going to ask to look at page 2 of this document right away. On page 2 at the bottom of the document you can see the following: In Belgrade, 11th of June, 1998, this was signed by assistant minister, head of the department, Vlastimir Djordjevic. I'm also going to ask you to look at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll the document up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read in paragraph 9, what it says in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 9 it says: "Captain Milan Cankovic providing communications, equipment, vehicles and other equipment in the police administration of the ministry as the assistant staff leader for radio communications."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether this is you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And did you become a member of the staff on the basis of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the staff on the basis of this decision, but for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to speak about this in a minute. First, I would like to ask you to answer some questions in relation to this decision. First of all, let us go back to page 1 of the document. Can you read the title of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the composition of the staff leaders and members of the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. Can you please tell me to whom was this staff responsible for its work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The staff was responsible for its work directly to the chief of the department, to Lieutenant-General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we again look at page 2 of this document, please. Mr. Cankovic, if you look at the Roman numeral II, that paragraph, can you tell us who were the members of the expanded staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the expanded staff were the heads of secretariats of the interior in the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at these 14 persons that are mentioned in the decision, can you please tell me which departments they are from, all of these members of the Ministry of the Interior? If necessary, we can go back to page 1, if you need to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not needed. I am aware of the first page. All of the members were from the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. Earlier you said that on the basis of this decision, your term of duty was very brief. Can you please explain what you actually meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that already on the 16th of June, 1998, I received a new decision in which the minister of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia appointed me a member of the Kosovo and Metohija staff that was headquartered in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Exhibit P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before we look at that Exhibit, Mr. Cankovic, did you receive this decision personally that was issued by Mr. Djordjevic on the 11th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did personally receive both decisions. The decisions assigning me by the chief of the department, and also I personally received the minister's decision. I received this decision by the minister in Pristina though.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see on the screen in front of you something that I'm going to ask you to read, and that is the title of the decision of the 16th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Decision on the establishment of the ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask to see the last page of the decision. This is page 3 in both B/C/S and English. Mr. Cankovic, can you please tell us who signed this decision? Who issued the decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The decision was signed personally by Minister Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you to look at the persons referred to as the head, deputy head, and the members of this staff in the document. And when you look at the contents of page 1, please, let us know so we can continue to look at the names that are contained on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the staff was Major-General Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't need to read it, it's written down here. You can read it to yourself then I will put the question to you after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at page 2 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you look at these names, the names of the members of the staff, do you know in which MUP department these persons worked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: If we start from the Chief of Staff, he is from the public security department. His deputy was from the state security department. The commander of the special unit was from public security. The commander of the unit for special operations was from state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to continue. My question is whether staff members -- the staff members were from both departments of security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They were from both security departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. After the last named member, Dobrasin Krdzic, the paragraph below that refers to members of the extended staff. Can you please tell us who the members of this staff were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the expanded staff were the chief of secretariats for Internal Affairs centres and branches of the department of state security in the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. Can you please tell us if the chief of the public security department could issue instructions or orders to members of the state security department?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't do that in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me who could issue instructions and orders to members of both departments.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: This could be done only by the head of both departments, and that was only the minister of the Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. Can you look at the same decision and the same page. Can you look at the paragraph marked with Roman II. When you look at that, just read it to yourself, and you can give us a brief comment on whether what is written there was actually put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In brief, what was the role of the staff for the suppression of terrorism in the area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: To organise and control the work in that domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did this entail all units of the Ministry of the Interior in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: We could see from the document itself that it applied to all the units of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija, those participating in anti-terrorist operations as well as the regular force belonging to the respective secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you refer to the units participating in anti-terrorist operations, what units do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The units which participated in anti-terrorist operations were the PJP Units, the SAJ, as well as the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll up in the Serbian, which is page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, I would kindly ask you to look at the Roman numeral III which is at the bottom of your page. Tell me this: Who was the staff answerable to, that is to say, the person in charge of the staff had to report to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: We can see from paragraph 3 that the staff was answerable directly to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see here who they were obliged to report to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The staff had to report to the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia who established it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. One other thing, before we move on to the next page of the document, let's do that first. The next page is actually the last page in both versions. We could see what is stated in the decision. Did it work in practice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at paragraph 6 which is the last paragraph of the document. In the first sentence it is stated: "With the coming into force of this decision, the following shall cease to be valid:" And we have a number of decisions listed. Do we also see the decision of the 11th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's here. As well as the decision of -- yes, that's what the decision actually ends with, with that particular decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. Between the 16th of June, 1998, and the date when the staff was established by the minister, all the way until the units withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija, was there any other minister of the interior staff in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no other staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your immediate superior in 1998 and 1999, and I mean between June 1998 and June 1999 in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior during that period, because I was a chief in his staff, was the head of the staff General Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you were a chief in his staff, what were you the chief of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: As we can see from the decision, I was the chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: During 1998 and 1999, did you receive all orders solely from the head of the staff for the suppression of terrorism in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija? I have the same period in mind.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to put a number of general questions about the functioning of the staff whose member you were. First of all, where was the seat of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The seat of the staff was in Pristina. To be precise, for awhile we were in the secretariat building in Pristina which was before the air campaign, and after that we changed locations, although the staff was always in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How frequently were the staff meetings held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Meetings of the staff were in a way held daily when circumstances allowed, but when there were anti-terrorist operations underway, such meetings were not held while they lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the bombing, the situation was completely different because there were interruptions in communications, lines, and our inability to use any communications means. We had to rely on slow courier connections, and we couldn't exchange information in a fast and efficient way. Hence, meetings were held seldom. However, certain chiefs of secretariats and other staff came to the staff whenever an opportunity arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Who attended the staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The staff meetings were always attended by the head of the staff, his deputy, and assistants along their professional lines, as well as chiefs within their respective domains. That was for the most part the composition of such staff meetings in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the decisions we could see that mention was made of an expanded staff. What did that entail?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The extended staff had weekly meetings. There were members of the staff present headed by the head and his deputy, as well as secretariat chiefs from the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. Next, there were unit commanders and PJP Units, as well as the SAJ commanders and the JSO commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the situation change once the air campaign began as opposed to what it was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course the situation was no longer the same. There were less members in attendance. For example, there were some secretariat chiefs who only managed to reach the staff and its head once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any working hours of the staff? And if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were regular working hours in normal conditions. The staff worked between 8.00 a.m. and 3.00 p.m., then there would be a break, and then it would work again between 7.00 and 9.00 p.m., and between 9.00 p.m. and 8.00 a.m., there was always a duty officer there, and that duty officer was either the deputy head of the staff or one of the chiefs. Of course, these working hours did not apply in the course of operations because then the staff worked round the clock for as long as such operations lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Who headed those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, all meetings were held by the chief of the staff and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the names?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Sreten Lukic and his deputy, Mr. Gajic, who was there on behalf of the state security department of sector. In Mr. Gajic's absence, Mr. Vilicic. Was usually there. But I think it was already 1999 that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did such meetings usually last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part we tried to keep them as short as possible because of other obligations that the staff members had. If the expanded staff sat, that included unit commanders who also had their respective duties. On average it would be between one and two hours. When we had sessions of the expanded staff it would usually take longer because secretariat chiefs usually submitted oral reports on the situation in the field, and in such situations, meetings took longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend all of the meetings of the staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Due to the amount of work I had, I seldom attended such meetings, but I was always kept informed of all the tasks issued to me. I would receive them from other members of the staff who took notes of what was important for me. These were usually Mr. Adamovic or Mr. Mijatovic. This is how we co-operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your specific tasks in the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: My task first and foremost was to secure communication between the staff and field units. When I say communication, I mean radio communication. This also included phone lines, but there wasn't that much work to be done there because the secretariat in Pristina had their own communications department, and following my instructions they assigned telephone lines. As for radio communication, I took direct part in that part of the work, and it was mostly led by me. My task was to enable co-operation between the staff and the communications administration, as well as to set up radio channels for operations, to draft call lists and reprogramme radio sets, and a number of other things. But most of my time was spent doing the things I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with each of the tasks you mentioned, but before that, tell me whether you submitted reports to anyone concerning your work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: If you have in mind oral reports, I did, daily, after each and every task. If you have in mind any written reports, then I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you report to orally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: To the chief of the staff. To the head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the reprogramming of radio sets, what do you have in mind? What type of task was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: When PJP Units were engaged, which had come into Kosovo and Metohija, they had to bring along their regular radio sets which they otherwise used in their respective secretariats. Those radio sets were not programmed so as to be compatible with the system we used in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. We had much work there to reprogramme them to have our standard channels preset as well as operational channels used exclusively by the staff and to preset a command channel in addition to the regular and operational channels as well as to introduce the so-called simplex type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And you also mentioned setting up an operations radio channel, and now in your answer again you refer to the command channel or the channel for operations. Can you please explain what these channels are and how did you set them up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija there was a radio network, regular radio network. The radio network worked on that principle for actions. So when we are talking about one type of network, we can talk about the other type. One was a regular network and the other one was an action network. The first one was permanent and the other one was on an as-needed basis. Each detachment had its own channel when going off on an anti-terrorist action. It was a unique channel that everybody had, and that also included the head of the staff, the Chief of Staff. There were also channels of the semi-duplex type which could function in micro locations. So this was the basis on which it functioned. These repeaters and channels of the units that were operational would be used as needed, and they were on repeaters or relays where you also had the equipment for regular channels. They went through the same channels. These were just regular facilities. For example, above Prizren we had a station at Sara then near Djakovica. We had the repeater station at Cabrat. If we are talking about Pec, we had such a facility at Mokra Gora. The one for Pristina was at Butovacki Breg. The one that covered Giljane was at Zeleni Vrh. Urosevac was covered by Bukova Glava, and there was a joint channel on Bukova Glava for all the secretariats that converged towards Pristina, towards the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you for a clarification. When you are setting up an operations communications network, who can participate in this network and in what manner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The radio communications during anti-terrorist operation or actions for specific areas would have specific facilities. For example, if it was Kosovo, the repeater station at Mokra Gora would be active -- I'm sorry, did I say the Kosovo area or the Metohija area? Let's say Metohija, that area would use the repeater station at Mokra Gora and the one at Vukovar Glava, the one at Cabrat above Djakovica. Now, since there were many mountainous rugged areas and it wasn't possible for some parts of units to be able to communicate all the time and on the basis of the type of terrain that the action would be carried out on, I had confirmation repeater station. I would decide on lower elevations where I would set up such repeater stations in order to reinforce the communication system. We had these semi-duplex type of communications that proceeded via repeater stations. Of course units could communicate amongst themselves at some micro locations using the simplex type of communications, but this is something that has a shorter range.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We will come back to this in more detail. Just a small digression, how did all of this function after the NATO bombing began?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: After the bombing began and the radio relay facilities in Kosovo and Metohija were destroyed, it actually didn't function. The systems were destroyed. There was no power supply, and it was not possible to maintain these communications, and they were downed. There was only communication via radio that could be supported through mobile repeater stations, and they covered a much smaller area than the earlier repeater stations would be able to cover when they were in working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the very beginning when we are talking about actions, and then we will come to this particular thing. So then I would ask you to provide a more specific example illustrating how all of this functioned. First of all, can you please tell us how you received assignments in the staff relating to anti-terrorist actions that would be conducted in the area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Once actions were planned, once these plans were completed, and once the section where a certain action would take place would be established, I would then receive maps from Mr. Adamovic or Mr. Mijatovic, excerpts of maps, topographical maps where the axis of movement of specific units would be marked. On the basis of that, I would figure out the area where -- the area that needed to be covered by a radio network.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your answer once the plans were complete. Are you aware who planned these actions? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The actions were planned by the chief, the deputy chief, the operations chief of the staff, including Mr. Mijatovic and Mr. Adamovic. And as needed, very often some others would be invited to participate. Some commanders, for example, or commanders of the PJP or the SAJ Units or the JSO Units depending on the terrain where they were for possible suggestions that they could make, but they didn't participate in the planning all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you take part in these planning actions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you know if there was any co-ordination between the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP staff in these planning activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, there was, because Adamovic or Mijatovic were mostly communicating with the corps in Pristina where the Army of Yugoslavia was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as communications are concerned, I'm, first of all, thinking of the relationship between the army and the police and the communications that the MUP had and that the army had. What was the relationship between these two networks? Were they compatible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm really not familiar with the system of communications that they had, they were carrying them with them. But I really didn't know what sort of equipment they were. We had our radio stations that the commanders in the field carried. The co-operation mostly boiled down to perhaps some superior officer of the army being together with the police unit or vice-versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me if there was a possibility for the Army of Yugoslavia to use the frequencies used by the police or for the police to use frequencies used by the army, and for these communications to intersect or to be used together?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, this wasn't possible and never was possible. Generally, according to the frequency division plan, this is not permitted. According to the general plan, the army had its own range of frequencies, and the army and the police had their own, the railway system had its own, the PTT services had their own range of frequencies, so you could never combine these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And now that we are talking about equipment, did the police use similar equipment in its communication system as the army in its communication system?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The army was always big and inert in comparison to us, and this probably applies to every army, I'm not going to go into that. So their system of communications was based on the radio relay system. It was a completely different communication signal system from ours. They probably had more of that kind of communications in their vehicles, in their transporters, but I really don't know how their system functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us more or less how the actions were planned, but can you tell us how the preparations for these actions were carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, preparation for action is more of a different activity than this one because in preparation for the action, people would assemble in the staff who were in charge of the action. This would be the Chief of Staff, deputy Chief of Staff, then you would get the commander of the Special Police detachments, the commander of the special anti-terrorist unit, the commander of the unit for special operations, the chiefs of the secretariats. Especially those from the secretariat would participate in the area where the action would be carried out. This would be the broader composition, and then the planning and the assignment of tasks would take some more time. The participants in the actions would also address these meetings. This is how I understood it to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And did you attend these preparatory meetings often?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: When they were making their plans and agreements, I was already out in the field. I was already making preparations. Before they would get together, I already would have received my working assignments, which I extracted from the map, which they used later, and then together with my group of technicians and communications people, we would go and carry out our assignments. Excuse me, yeah, because this is what we had to do. We had to be prepared at a specific time. For example, if the action would begin at 5.00 a.m., I already had to have everything ready by 3.00 a.m. Everything had to be ready before.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the situation when the NATO bombing began? Did things work in exactly the same way as you have just described, or can you please specify when preparations were carried out in this way that you just described?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, this couldn't be. It couldn't be done any more because members of the narrow inner staff and the expanded staff couldn't actually get together.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they couldn't meet and that things were different, which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And how were tasks assigned, or how were units informed about their tasks at the time, how were preparations carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time we tried to do something by using mobile radio communication systems, but later this became very dangerous, especially with the destruction of the repeater stations. Any sources of radiation became dangerous. So we did it with a lot of fear, and then once -- if we had to do it, then we would do it anyway but then we would try to stay as far away from these facilities as possible. Mostly the communications were done by courier. That was how it was done in that period. For example, the messenger for Prizren would have to go and come back conveying his message two or three times a day because the message would be urgent. So this is how our communications were then proceeding in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say command channel, what do you mean by that, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The command channel was used by commanders of detachments or units in the field, I'm talking about police units now. They were connected directly to the Chief of Staff. Only commanders of those units in the field could use that channel, and the staff chief. Each unit, as I said, also had their own repeater stations and then if they were in some broader area of a company or so, then they had their own internal repeater station, just like the secretariats each had their own internal repeater stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us which units took part or were participants in this command channel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Just like I said in the beginning, these were units that were carrying out actions. These were the PJP, SAJ, and JSO Units.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me after the anti-terrorist action would be completed, was this command channel -- or did this command channel or these communications set up specially for that particular action cease to operate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: This action radio network would stop functioning as soon as the units returned to their starting positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell me, this action radio network, was it set up for each individual anti-terrorist action that was carried out in the area of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, for each one. If we are talking about anti-terrorist actions which were larger, which encompassed larger swathes of territory and if they included several units. However, the same thing applied in actions with just one company or one detachment. Actually, they would then mostly use the simplex type of communication. They would communicate amongst each other because this would be in a village or a smaller town. And they would have a working channel, regular working channel connecting them to the staff, so in case of any kind of emergency or anything, they could use this regular channel. And ultimately it was their duty to call in in case of any kind of intervention or if they had a call from the Chief of Staff or deputy Chief of Staff. And I can mention that in the situation when regular radio communications were used, where all secretariats could listen in, then scrambled communications, scrambling would be used for precaution sake and only short messages would be relayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you partake directly in the actions for which you were charged to set in place a radio communications system on the action channel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I left nothing to chance. When a repeater system which used relay station could be employed, and this was the case where operations took place in a flat area and where radio stations could be normally used, I would be on standby to make sure that units did not use channels they were not designated to use. However, where an operation involved a larger swath of territory and where an operation was of a larger scale, which involved rugged terrain, and made it possible for units to find themselves in areas where radio communications would not operate because of the various obstacles, I would put in place the so-called mobile repeaters. Since it was otherwise impossible for me to set up stations of this sort, I had to follow the unit and set up repeaters for micro locations. I don't know on how many occasions this must have been, but at least six or seven, eight times I was in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cankovic, do you know up until what time in 1998 were anti-terrorist operations conducted in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, to make it simple for you, up until what period of time were you in charge of setting up these action radio communication systems you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in late September or early October already that the radio stations that were in the outlying area such as Sviljen and Mokra Gora, which were difficult to reach, and it was already cold, I dismantled the radio communication systems since no more operations were expected. At least this is what we were told. I dismantled the stations and took all the equipment along, and I can tell you that my radio communication systems were no longer used.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in October of 1998 the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that under the agreement verifiers were expected to arrive in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not I myself, save for the chance encounters in the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the month of October up until the start of the NATO bombing, did you take part in any of the operations in Kosovo and Metohija, and did you set up any action communication systems in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've told you, I no longer engaged in any such activity. I had by that time dismantled all of my equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, did your duties and assignments change in any way after the start of NATO bombing on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. As I said, mobile repeaters were used in order to have radio communication systems up and running. However, it did not help much. I was very much engaged in the relocation of the staff which changed locations at the time. And this had to be done. The radio communications were operational until the SUP building was hit, and this was the first major obstacle we were confronted with.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get back to that later. Tell me, on how many occasions during the bombing was the Pristina staff relocated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to draw a clear distinction because the staff per se was never housed in one location. When it comes to the staff leader, well, they changed location at least ten times, perhaps even more. Since the staff would normally be housed in two or three locations, segments of it would be relocated, but other segments not that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were all these locations where elements of the staff were housed equipped with radio communication systems?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: During bombing when we started relocating the staff, up until the 29th, it was still possible for the Pristina communications department to provide telephone lines and special telephone lines for the staff leader and all the other members of the staff, including the telegraphy, because the SUP building was used where all these lines were up and running. We also had the radio sets, but we only had receivers, not transmitters. If we wanted to use transmitters, then it had to be done elsewhere. And this was, of course, for security reasons to protect the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the special telephone line is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The special telephone line is one used in the secretariat or in the Ministry of the Interior. There was a certain degree of protection involved because the switchboards for the various telephone lines were in the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior unlike the ordinary telephone lines which had their switchboards in post offices. We had this special telephone line in the Ministry of the Interior, and we had hired a special line from the telecommunications company, and that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What became of the communications systems as of the start of the bombing on the 24th of March? You mentioned the 29th. Can you specify which month it was, and what happened with the communications system?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 29th of March that the secretariat building in Pristina was destroyed. At that point all the special lines that existed with these secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija and the ministry and other secretariats across Serbia were down. The telegraph was not operational, which meant that dispatches could no longer be sent from the staff and the secretariat in Pristina to all the other secretariats. In other words, what remained were only local radio networks, and especially so later on when Butovacki Breg and Goles were destroyed. Butovacki Breg was not that important but Goles was because the telegraph and telephone system which covered Serbia went through that particular station.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened after the 29th of March, what were the developments that followed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after the 29th of March, we were practically left only with the local switchboards, and we had some sort of radio communications in Pristina and through the PTT. We had communications with the secretariats and the ministry up until the point when the post office building was destroyed, at which point the regular telephone lines across the town were also destroyed. None of the secretariats were in contact with Pristina any longer and vice-versa. The line with Belgrade was established through the existing optic cable, which was relocated to the new switchboard, as it was called at the time. The optical line was established via Nis and on to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, from that point on, what was the means of communications used by the staff combatting anti-terrorist activity with units that were deployed in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. The interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, the interpreters didn't hear your answer. Can you please repeat your answer to my question. What was the means of communications used by the staff combatting anti-terrorist activity with units in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: If we are referring to the period following bombing and the destruction of the various buildings, that is to say, the building of the secretariat and post office in Pristina, the only reliable means of communications was through couriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the means of communication used by the staff with the ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The staff communicated with the minister through the optic cable which went from Pristina via Nis on to Belgrade. But let me tell you this, this cable did not belong to the MUP of Serbia. It was only the optic cable used by the telecom of Serbia, and many town lines were connected to it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I see that my question was interpreted as being what was your communication with the ministry in Belgrade, whereas, I asked what was your communication with the minister, and that's the answer you gave us. Now, this communication that ran through the optic cable, was it used by the Pristina staff, could it be used by the staff itself to communicate with the minister in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Since there were quarters of town where communication systems were destroyed, there could be no communications directly from the location where the optic cable was initially connected. We tried to use locations where we could get connected to and have communication. Wherever elements of the staff, including the staff leader were housed, they had this connection, and they had the possibility to use the communication system.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What types of communication could be used by way of this cable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could transmit verbal messages over the telephone line and written messages by use of facsimile, a fax machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who it was that the staff leader informed after the NATO forces started bombing the area, that is to say, after the month of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Before and after bombing, he always informed or reported to the minister and was always in contact with him. He would report to him about the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, about the conduct of operations. He would always report directly to the minister, and this was the situation both before and after bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How come you know this, Mr. Cankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know this because on several occasions I would be the duty officer in the staff. I had to be there as a communications officer to make sure that the system was always up and running. It was not his duty to be in that particular location at all times. He could abruptly decide to relocate the staff, in which case I would be duty-bound to put a communication system in place. Normally, he would choose a location where the system was already operational. And wherever a minister would be -- wherever a call would be placed for the minister, I would be there to respond, and I'm talking about situations where he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, your answer has not been interpreted fully. Can you please repeat your answer. How do you know this? You said that the staff leader communicated directly with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I personally heard the staff leader, Mr. Lukic, talk to the minister, not once but several times. Even I myself when I was a duty officer by the telephone line when the staff leader was absent received calls from the minister who told me that Lukic should return the call as soon as he got back.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, did you know whether the head of the staff informed anyone else about things save for the minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard him do that, and I don't think there was any need for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that some dispatches were sent to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Dispatches could not have been sent any other way save by facsimile. I do know that. But I'm not familiar with the contents of any dispatches though. I must say this, though, we could only transmit poor copies and for the most part we ended up resorting to the use of couriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I think this is a good time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now. We must have an adjournment now for half an hour. We resume at 4.15. A Court Officer will assist you in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, did you keep radio station logs or phone books for such channels that you set up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what these station lists or logs were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Such logs for different channels were used basically for the same purpose, as one would for regular radio channels used by the secretariats. All units, all PJP Units, that is, as well as all SAJ Units and the JSO were in that log. They were each assigned a number of frequencies and channels they were to use. These channels and frequencies were permanent and the log was permanent throughout the duration of operations and the existence of operational channels. The only thing that differed was the unit that was in the field at that point in time. They had their respective log-books, and I never had to do this all over again. The only issue was how many units were in the field and then those units would use their respective code-names based on the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the process of drafting such logs, have you ever resorted to the use of code-name Morava?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was used as part of the regular log, and it was in use in Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: To have it reflected more accurately in the transcript, I wanted to ask you whether you used it in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the process of creation of operational logs, did you ever use the call-sign of Skorpioni?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you use the same call-signs on operational and regular channels?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the sense of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The staff had operational call-signs, and for the staff of the interior ministry, the call-sign in Pristina was Kosava in periods of operations. In regular conditions concerning the secretariats and regular tasks, the call-sign was Ruby or Rubin.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, in the course of 1998, did you see General Vlastimir Djordjevic in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija? And if so, when, on what occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 as of my arrival in Kosovo to the staff, I did see General Djordjevic on a few occasions. I saw him at least twice or three times in the field. I also saw him at least two or three or even four times in the Pristina SUP in the staff premises that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you see him in the field, if you can recall that? What were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: On those occasions when I saw him I believe them to be important. The first one was in Malisevo, I had a number of reasons to be with my union. The first reason was given that Malisevo is in the rear and could not effectively be reached by my repeater stations, I was supposed to set up a mobile repeater station. Secondly, if we -- in case of entering Malisevo, we were supposed to set up a duty operations office and set up a radio equipment in the OUP building which had previously been occupied by terrorists. Mr. Djordjevic was there when I saw him. That was on the first occasion I entered Malisevo. Another occasion was in the operation towards Klina and Jablanica and Glodjane. It was difficult terrain for radio communication, and I was there with some equipment. We entered a village and before that there had been a clash with the terrorists and the village was completely deserted. Afterwards there was no resistance whatsoever. On that occasion, we found basically all of the inhabitants in the mosque. It was in summertime. It was quite hot. And we reported that there were people in the mosque. Some commanders came and took them out. There were people fainting and there were children. It was not an easy scene. Mr. Djordjevic was there. We inquired who would be a representative of the village. They said that they were afraid of terrorists, and I supposed this was correct because the villages we went through before that were also deserted. So I believed people had pulled out. I particularly remember this one because of the grave situation with those people. We spent the night in that village, although I don't know whether Mr. Djordjevic did so. In any case, we sat down with the village representative, with the village elder, and had a discussion with him. I also saw him in the staff, although I had much to do and he was quite busy touring secretariats and units. Well, for the most part that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you refer to the village when you saw him, what village was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you saw him in the staff. Did Mr. Djordjevic attend the meetings of the staff in 1998 when you saw him in the staff building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic was not a staff member. He was under no obligation to attend any meetings of it. He did, however, come there on a number of occasions and he attended some meetings, but his presence had no particular effect, in the sense that he wasn't there to deal with anything in particular. Of course, he held consultations and things like that, but that was the extent of it. In the secretariat building, he had a small office. I know that because I had installed a regular phone line in his office. We did not install a special line because he wasn't there permanently. Special lines were only assigned to officers who were in their office all time. For him, however, this was just a side office.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1999, did you see General Djordjevic in Kosovo and Metohija, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 I saw Mr. Djordjevic -- the minister was there then as well because there was a government session in Kosovo. I saw the prime minister, the late Mirko Marjanovic there, as well as a number of other ministers. I remember we lined up in front of the secretariat building, and we reported to Mr. Marjanovic, the prime minister. I'm positive that Mr. Djordjevic was there as well. On that day I went to Belgrade. I was planned to go the day before that because I had to take over some equipment there. However, I was asked to stay and they were even jokingly telling me that I could join the government on their plane back to Belgrade. I do remember that I was supposed to bring some equipment back. That was sometime in the morning, perhaps around 10.00 or 11.00 or perhaps around noon. In any case, they all went to attend the government meeting, and I was told that they were to go to Belgrade afterwards. As for any tasks of mine in that regard, they were completed by the time of that meeting and I went to Belgrade. In any case, I did see Mr. Djordjevic on that occasion. That was the only time I saw him in 1999 in Kosovo and Metohija. If we are talking about the time when I was in the staff, I also saw him on, say, another couple of occasions. One of them was during a trip similar to the one I just referred to. It was in Belgrade in their so-called staff. In the staff where the minister was, or rather, in that building in Lole Ribara Street -- well, at that time, they were in the building of Commercial de Banca. The chief of the communications administration also had his office there, and I came to see him three or four times, and on one such occasion I saw Mr. Djordjevic, or perhaps on two such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you are referring to submitting a report to Mr. Marjanovic, the prime minister, can you tell me who reported to him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was on those staffs a number of times and reports were usually given by such officers who had completed military academies. In this particular case, it was Adamovic. However, during a previous period it was Colonel Arsenijevic. In any case, on this occasion it was Adamovic. He submitted his report to the PM Mirko Marjanovic in the presence of the minister of the interior, Vlajko Stojilkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that it was in the morning at around 10.00 or 11.00 or perhaps at around noon. Can you be any more precise than that, if you can, of course?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Not from this point in time, I can't be any more precise. I don't think it was around noon. It was probably sometime before that, although I don't know when. First of all, we waited for the plane to land, and we were in front of the building throughout that time. In any case, time passed slowly, and I do not have a clear memory of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see P144 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, on your screen you will see a decision. It says: "As of 31 May 1999, Captain Milan Cankovic, employee of the Ministry of the Interior police administration shall cease to carry out special security related tasks in the MUP staff in Pristina where he was deployed on 1 May [as interpreted] 1998." Mr. Cankovic, did your duties in the MUP staff or the suppression of terrorism in Pristina cease by virtue of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in the transcript, line 8 it states from the 1st of May, 1998, but it should say from the 1st of June 1998. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, during 1998 and 1999, did you ever see or hear of any plan or agreement within the Ministry of Internal Affairs according to which the population -- the Albanian population would be expelled from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: During 1998 or 1999 did you see or hear of any plan or agreement in the Ministry of Internal Affairs to expel the Albanian population and thereby change the ethnic structure of the population in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, did you mean May 1998, June 1998, or the year 1999 when you corrected the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I corrected the transcript, I was thinking of the 1st of June, 1998, because that is what the date is in the document, the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We may be looking at something different. We are seeing the year 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see anywhere 1999 in the English translation. The mistake is 1st of May, 1998, and it should correctly read the 1st of June, 1998. This is what it says in the original, and in the English I can see that the date says the 1st of May, 1998. It should correctly be the 1st of June, 1998. The date I'm talking about is in paragraph 2 of the decision where it says, is no longer going to be carrying out the duties in the police administration. The document -- as of 1st of June, 1998. The document is dated the 30th of May, 1999. Your Honours, a brief explanation. Mr. Cankovic was sent on the 1st of June, 1998, and the decision was dated the 1st of June, 1998. With this decision, he is no longer being assigned to the post from the 1st of June, 1998. So the decision whereby he is no longer supposed to be at that assignment is the 1st of May, 1999. The English translation in paragraph 2 should state the 1st of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think we understand what you are saying, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the original the date seems to be 01.06.1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. Thank you, Mr. Cankovic. Your Honours, I have now completed my examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, if I could just have one second to set up the podium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Take two if you need.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. In 1998 on a day-to-day basis, what were some of the usual tasks that you would perform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, well, we can split that into two periods. Until the 1st of October and from the 1st of October. Up until the 1st of October, as we said, actions were being conducted against Albanian terrorists, and in those kinds of assignments -- well, you heard mostly about those kinds of assignments. I don't have anything particular more to say about that. After the 1st of October, after the agreement that the Verification Missions should be sent to the Kosovo and Metohija area, I no longer had any tasks in that area. During that period, I had assignments relating to the withdrawal or the pulling out of equipment which was located in the places which I referred to earlier. And I can say a little bit more about that. So there was quite a lot of equipment there. Then my other assignments were to get the equipment back, store it. Units were still changing over, and they spent 45 days in the field and then switched, and this was happening continuously. The units were not all being changed at the same time. So I always had new units, I had to issue instructions, direct them in their work so I had work also in the staff itself. These were my duties roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You spoke about setting up radio communications out in the field during an action prior to October of 1998. When you would set up these radio communications, who could receive and listen into that channel within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: We had communications on channels that were not used for regular radio communication. These were channels dedicated -- actually, these were channels on a different frequency range from the usual one, if that means anything. The regular radio network used by the secretariats within Kosovo, and this also applies to the Serbia as a whole, this was done on VHF. My systems of communications were ultrashort UHF, and it was set up where there were already repeater stations and relay stations which were either military, post office, or TV channels. So in that sense, the radio communications that I was setting up were used only by the units for anti-terrorist actions. The ones that I mentioned, this was the PJP, the SAJ, and the JSO, they were using those communications. Those communications were used from the moment that an action was launched and were used only until the end of the action and the return of the units to their, let's say, home base. After that the communication system was dismantled and not used anymore. These communications could only be followed, exclusively be followed by people from these units and by those in the staff in Pristina. Of course some undesirable elements could also monitor these communications, but we didn't really record any intrusions or incursions into our communications network. I never had an occasion to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So just to make sure that I understand, during the operation, the units involved in the operation could listen to this radio station or channel, I'm not sure the technical term, and also the staff in Pristina was also able to hear it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Not listen in, but participate and work on that channel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, moving to the NATO bombing. What were the regular tasks that you would perform on a day-to-day basis during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the bombing, my primary assignments were, just like in regular conditions, to secure existing and possibly new communications for the staff with units that were out in the field as much as possible and with the ministry, the minister that the staff was accountable to. That was the primary task. Secondary tasks were to have everything that needed to be done by the units in the field which were constantly moving in terms of maintenance or repair we would do. They would bring this equipment to us, and this we would describe as kind of on-going, daily work. So I was mostly sticking close to the staff and making sure in all possible ways that these communications were functioning properly. In the beginning there were situations when this equipment that we had, I'm talking about the mobile communications equipment, the same equipment that was being used at the relay stations and which was now being used at some lower elevations for security reasons because of the bombing, and this was quite dangerous because any kind of emission of vibrations, frequency, or energy was a possible target, so we would repair or go to those facilities only when this was essential. But these type of communications were not used on a regular basis. They were not permanent. They were something that posed quite a danger, so people who had to deal with issues with that type of equipment were quite concerned and were exposed to a considerable amount of danger while performing these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether in Belgrade they had their own communication staff there to perform a similar function to you to make sure that their communications were working in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't have a communications staff in Belgrade. You could only have communications that would be attached to the staff, and that's what did exist. And I did say earlier that I saw Mr. Djordjevic at that staff sometimes. I had to make a connection between him and the Belgrade centre. So you had the chief of that communication centre sitting there. In a way, I was the main person in the area, and the person who is in charge of these communications would always be close to the staff. As opposed to us, let's say that that staff had a little bit more room and possibility to set up communications with other staffs because the main post office in Belgrade was not knocked down, so the possibility of having normal telephone calls, not special telephone communications, was working. And the system for special telegraph and telephone connections was destroyed. So all they had at their disposal was just regular telephone communications, telephone lines, but they had much more potential or capacity than we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I see Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have an objection exclusively to the transcript. I'm listening to what Mr. Cankovic was saying, and line 22 absolutely does not correspond to what he said in the Serbian. I actually never heard that sentence at all. Perhaps it could cause some confusion. It's quite general. I agree that in the Serbian the witness absolutely did not say that and that could give rise to some further questions that I would just like to warn the counsel or the Chamber, I don't know whether she believes that this is something that would need to be further clarified or established, but simply this was not stated in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen, page 41 in the area of line 22, I leave it to you whether you see it as of significance or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to clarify your answer a bit in a couple of ways. Initially I thought I understood you to say there was not a communication staff in Belgrade who dealt with communication issues, but as your answer continued, it seems that there is a communication staff in Belgrade. Could you just explain whether there exists people who deal with communication issues in Belgrade much as you did in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you the first time and I understood you now, but you need to understand me. There is no communication staff. Only there is a communication facility in the staff. Just like I am a representative for the communications in the Pristina staff, there is a communications representative at the staff in Belgrade, the staff where the minister is. In that staff we had Mr. Vasilije Joksic who was the chief of the communications administration for Serbia. Down in the staff is where I was sitting pursuant to a decision by the minister where I was the chief of communications for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you handled Kosovo and Metohija. There was a different individual who dealt with this in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, the transcript earlier quoted you as saying that you had seen Mr. Djordjevic, I believe, in the -- let's see what the exact word is. It says: "And I did say earlier that I saw Mr. Djordjevic at that staff. Sometimes I had to make a connection between him and the Belgrade centre. So you had the chief of that communication centre sitting there." Was that an accurate translation of what you said, and if not, you can feel free to correct that at this point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the translation is not correct. I could not set up a communication in Belgrade for Mr. Djordjevic. My job was to set up a communication line to the Chief of Staff in Pristina and the other members of the staff who were not at the same place. For example, you had three or four locations where parts of the staff were. So I was trying and I was successful in securing communications for all of them which after the post office was bombarded in Boles [as interpreted] consisted of telephone communications which was made from the town post office in Pristina using optic cable which went through Nis to Belgrade. That was the communication line which was used by the Pristina post office and the parts of town which were connected to that exchange. So let's understand each other. This was not a communication of the SUP, the MUP, the army. It was a way to relay communications via the PTT Serbia facilities. So we were the users of those telephones and those numbers. The telephones were city telephones, the phone numbers were city telephone numbers, there was no special connection. Thus, I could only secure communications to the chief of the staff and parts of the staff in Pristina, whereas Mr. Joksic with his departments and work lines, in this case, this was, you know, only the section for telephone traffic, he would provide communications to the minister and the members of the staff at the ministry in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in this trial, we've heard from a Mr. Deretic. Do you know Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Deretic. At the time I was in Pristina, Deretic was the chief of the communications department in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And he testified that it was the responsibility of the communications department in Pristina, it was his responsibility to take on responsibility for SUPs throughout Kosovo. Are you aware of that also?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew about it and of course that is correct. So I was assigned, as I said at the beginning, to a chief communications amongst units in the field and the Chief of Staff or the staff in Pristina, that was my main activity. I said that at the very beginning. Mr. Deretic was taking care of and taking care so about the system of communications which was used in peacetime. For all secretariats, he was in charge of telephone communications, telegraph communications. He was in charge of special telephone communications. All that was under the SUP and the secretariats Milos Deretic was in charge of. So I'm only saying that this when we were working on that to secure telephone radio communications for the Chief of Staff and other members of the staff, of course that was something that had to be done by Milos Deretic, but I was also there to decide when and where a certain communication would be installed. In that sense, if you understood me literally, that I was the one doing that, that I was the bearer of the telephone exchange, that is not so. But I plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
