utterances.text: Can you explain your responsibility -- you mentioned the duty centre. During the NATO bombing, what was your job responsibility with regard to the duty centre, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the duty centre. Nothing whatsoever. Because the duty centre is something that is a permanent body and had to be constantly present. So I could never be sure that I would be in one place for the next half an hour or so, so I could never be a member of any kind of duty centre. If you saw from my testimony, I was very rarely at these, how shall I put it, meetings about preparations, the work, and let me put it that way, these actions and all that kind of thing. But I was a participant in that in the sense that I was the one who was securing communications for those units that were operating in the field. And I explained the way in which I did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, during the NATO bombing at what location did you generally work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question specifically. Which locations do you mean? You mean the locations where the staff was or which locations where I was doing what? If we are talking about locations where I was working for the staff, that was, for example, like I said, you know, the staff itself changed at least ten locations. I'm thinking about the chiefs of staff, members of the staff depending on what they were doing in order not to disturb one another and ultimately it was not desirable to have the entire staff in one place for security reasons. These others, let me put it that way, other parts of the staff, we did not really change over so much. But I was obliged to monitor whether the communications were provided, whether this was working properly, and sometimes, if necessary, and this is something that I said in the beginning and this was being like that for awhile only in that initial period after all of these bombings and all of that, it was necessary to do something with that radio communications network, for example, some of these places with these mobile repeater stations, yes, but this was really brief, and I really cannot take credit for that kind of work myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this way: How often were you actually in an office setting, and how often were you out in the field? I guess I'm wondering, were you more travelling to different areas, fixing radio towers or fixing technical equipment away from an office, or were you more located in an office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: This may sound rather impossible to you, but it was, as I say, in addition to the jobs I've just referred to, I also visited the secretariats. If you can take my word for it, I went through certain zones which were not controlled by the police in order to arrive at a different secretariat, and if I had to do that, I did. Whether I was crazy enough to do that or not, that's for someone else to judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, were you travelling around to these secretariats most of the time, or were you usually in Pristina in an office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, I spent a lot of time in various offices. For example, the head of the staff would leave and there were none of those who were supposed to stand in for him along professional lines, then I would assume that duty. I was part of technical personnel. There was always someone next to him in charge of police and operational work. I frequently stayed to replace him while, for example, he attended a meeting in a different part of the staff. In any case, my job was --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I could just stop you there. Are you saying that you stood in for Lukic when he was absent? That you were acting as the chief of the MUP staff in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Wherever Lukic went, he had a telephone line available. If an office had been assigned to him and if there was a regular city line there, if he went to another building and someone called him back to the other office, someone was supposed to be there to tell that person that Mr. Lukic was in the field and absent. I could only act as his secretary of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: How often would you do that? It sounds like you were quite busy, so how much did you have time to just sit in an office and answer phone calls?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: During the last period I tried to spend as much time as possible in the office, but I couldn't really.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I mean how much time did you spend sitting in Lukic's office while he was absent acting as his receptionist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I was only a receptionist. I could have been in Mijatovic's office, for example, while Mijatovic was absent and then someone would call him, and I was there to answer the phone and say that Mr. Mijatovic wasn't there and that a message could be left with me. Or I could tell that person at what number Mr. Mijatovic could be reached at. The head of the staff never told me where he went. He would either attend meetings in some other parts of the staff or something else, I can speculate whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to understand. You said earlier that you were in a lot of places. You were busy. You were running around dealing with things, and now you are telling us that you are spending time sitting in the office of other people answering their phones, and I'm just trying to understand how much of your time you spent doing that because it sounded like you were pretty busy.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was pretty busy, but since we are talking about offices, I never spent this much time in an office. I said that I would spend half an hour, an hour at a time in an office, but having this discussion with you one would believe that I spent at least half of my time during aggression in any office. I was in the first, second, or third office at any point in time, and it could just so happen that I would stay in the office with another staff member. It could just so happen that Mr. Lukic was not in his office all the time, and the minister wasn't in his office all the time in Belgrade either. In his absence someone was supposed to be there to take calls. In other words, there always needed to be someone on the end of the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to understand from you how much time you did that, and I think we need to break this down because your answer is a little confusing. First of all, did you yourself have an office? Your own office? Or were you sharing with a group of other people in the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I did not have an office of my own. My office at that time was wherever Mr. Lukic was and where the other parts of the staff were, but I was seldom in such premises. And when I say seldom, I have in mind, say, a 24-hour period. During such a period, I would spend perhaps an hour in an office, and the rest of the time, I was basically in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when you say, "at that time I did not have an office of my own. My office was wherever Mr. Lukic was," do you mean that your office was wherever his office was, not that you were constantly with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, you said that the MUP staff itself was often housed in different locations so when you say that, were you always in the location that Lukic was housed in when there was moving around?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic could never take up a different office or a building without previously consulting me. He could envisage any particular location, but if we could not introduce a telephone line there, it meant nothing. I was constantly with Lukic for that reason. And out of, say, three or four proposals he put forth about where he wanted to take shelter or an office, I first needed to check whether there was a possibility to establish phone lines and then I would assign him an office. I was always nearby as well because I never knew when he would want to change next.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, you just said you were constantly with him, with Lukic for that reason. I would just like to clarify that. I mean, it sounds like you would go, you would set up, if he was moving an office, you would set up the communication. Did you need to be around him any longer that it would take to do that, or is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I say that, when I say constantly with him, one would conclude that he changed offices every 20 minutes and that I was with him all time. But he would spend two or three or four days in a single location. In certain locations he spent as many as seven days. In the meantime there were other locations where lines had already been set up. This is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So just to be clear, you were not travelling around with General Lukic constantly, or in his presence on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I never travelled around with General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you stated, when you were answering questions from Mr. Popovic, that you did not take part in any of the planning of MUP operations or actions. So my question to you is: Your testimony, then, about how these actions were planned is not based on your firsthand knowledge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. And I wasn't interested in any such thing. I am not a true policeman so to say and I'm not an operative. I did take part in operations and in planning, but the planning of communication. If we see that as planning, then it is. Participation also is participation, however, but the planning of operations and their implementation in terms of combat, this is something I did not participate in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you also testified that you did not take part in the preparation of the operations other than your own work where you would go out into the field and you would have it set up by 3.00 a.m. if it started at 5.00 a.m. So your testimony about how the units involved would prepare, that's also not based on your own firsthand knowledge or experience; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, that is true. While I was in the field, commanders came to the staff and they would discuss the implementation of a plan. However, for me it was not important. The only thing important to me was the area where the operation was to take place. My clock started running as of the moment when the plan was complete. As soon as I received a definitely plan in the sense of area, the clock started running. If a plan was completed at noon and then there's a gathering of units and their discussion which goes on until 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. because they all have their own questions and the operation is, say, in the territory of Djakovica, I need to leave Pristina upon preparing all of the equipment to go in the field. I had a team of my own with which I worked on my part of the plan. Then I would draft my own plan. Based on that plan, depending on whether that was before the bombing or after or the time before February, I decided which repeater stations I would turn on, what other assets I needed, whether I needed mobile repeater stations and what personnel. Those were the details. Secondly, since each PJP detachment and the SAJ and JSO ... I had to get into touch. I had to check whether they had enough radio stations, but sometimes they didn't. It could just so happen that they too needed equipment. We also needed to work on the issues pertaining to the tasks those guys were supposed to carry out in the field as signalsmen. This was what the situation was like, and that's how things developed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, after an operation or an action was completed, would you receive any report about what happened during the action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. As I said, I participated three, four, or five times when I had to use mobile repeater stations. In other situation, my job was to decide the main feature such as the relay station at Mokra Gora. I would stay there and follow developments in the field from there in terms of radio communication. I was in touch with the signalsmen attached to the field units. That was my work. When there was redeployment or advancing or pulling out, when they left their units, their areas and could no longer be reached by their repeater stations, I would then direct the signalsman in question to use a different channel or a different repeater station belonging to another unit to establish communication. That was my work throughout operations. When an operation was finished, I would stay at the feature awaiting the return of the units to their deployment area. Their commanders would then go to the staff working probably on the -- their reports. In the meantime, I would dismount my equipment and go back. If the operation took until 4.00, 5.00, or 6.00 p.m., I couldn't reach the staff before 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. I could only receive new tasks from Mijatovic or Adamovic if there was to be the continuation of that action the next day. Or if there was other operation, plans would be drafted anew and the whole story began again. If an operation took several days, I would be in a single location, much as I was during operations which took only a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: As chief of communications for the MUP staff, what kind of reporting did you personally receive, if any? I don't mean to suggest that there was any, but if you did, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I never received any reports from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I think that you said in your testimony that you also were not familiar with the content of MUP dispatches?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I did not send a dispatch, I was not familiar with its contents, and I had no right to be, or unless I was one of the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, did you generally read MUP dispatches?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Firstly, there was no time. Secondly, I had no interest in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You also said in your testimony that you didn't write any written reports to anyone, but you would give oral reports to General Lukic. Could you just tell us briefly what the general subject matter of those reports would cover.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: When we say that I gave reports to Mr. Lukic, I meant to say that he was my superior and I was under an obligation to plan or comment on communications issues. However, he wasn't privy to it in the sense that this was not part of his work. In that sense, I could not submit a report to him, because to him it meant nothing. Communications were in order. The staff was content with the work I did, and I was part of that staff during the previous period. I had three or four terms of service with that staff. I was familiar with the area. I was familiar with the profession, and I enjoyed their full support. The same went for Deretic in his domain. He could never submit reports to me. He did his work, and he could receive reports in turn because he was a chief too. However, I as a chief was under no obligation to report to anyone, not even the communications administration in Belgrade because I was in a staff where the minister was. There was a line of command. Lukic was my superior and the minister was superior to him. That was the end of it. As to how they communicated and who gave what tasks to whom, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. You said in your testimony that you did not ever see the call-sign Morava used. This was also true in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us understand each other. The code-name of Morava is in the code-names log used by the secretariat in Pristina for their regular tasks. They were in touch with Morava. Morava was a duty office in the MUP of Serbia. It existed as such in the list of code-names, but of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. However, while on the topic of lists or logs, as well as operational logs, Morava never figured in any of my logs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I see we are approaching the time for the break. This would be a good time, if that's convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have the second break now. We resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that you seldom attended MUP staff meetings. So is it fair to say that your testimony about what when on in these MUP staff meetings was not your own firsthand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything I testified about concerning MUP staff meetings has it do with those meetings I attended. It is all firsthand knowledge. I'm not sure what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you seldom attended MUP staff meetings. About how many did you attend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: If you have in mind the meetings of the expanded staff, then there was one such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So your testimony is based on the one meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know in what part, but let's stay with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood what you just meant.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I attended one extended MUP staff meeting, and I testified about that based on that one meeting about that one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, in evidence in this case we have quite a few exhibits that are minutes of MUP staff meetings, and we've also heard some testimony from other witnesses about MUP staff meetings. And in the interests of time, I won't go through all of these with you, but I would just put to you that there are a number of these meetings in 1998 and 1999 where General Djordjevic is in attendance, where the security situation in Kosovo is discussed, and where plans about Kosovo are made. And my question to you is, you weren't necessarily in those meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did not participate in the making of any plans for Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. So at page 33 and 34 of the transcript where you stated that General Djordjevic in 1998 came to Kosovo but to no particular effect, you weren't in those meetings with him, so you really don't have firsthand knowledge of how he participated; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The question was whether I saw Mr. Djordjevic in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. I said I did, and I explained where. I said I saw him -- had I seen him at any meetings, I would have said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you stated an opinion at page 33 and 34 that General Djordjevic came to Kosovo for no particular effect. Now, because you weren't attending meetings with him, you don't really have a basis for saying that, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I thought I saw him. I said I did see him and I told you when and where.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. I think we are miscommunicating here, but I will move on. There is one exhibit that I'd like to show you from a MUP staff meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could have P689 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a meeting of a -- minutes of a meeting of a MUP staff for 2 December 1998. And in my review of these minutes, this was the one that I saw your name. Does this -- where I saw your name. Does this refresh your memory that this was the MUP staff meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we look at page 3 in both the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And I can just read it. Midway through the page, right after it says the meeting commenced: "Major General Sreten Lukic stated that on 27 November 1998 in Belgrade, a meeting at the Ministry of the Interior, which was chaired by minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, was attended by the chiefs of department for the public security and the state security, assistant ministers, head of the MUP staff in Pristina, and Nikola Sainovic. The current security situation in Kosovo was examined in the meeting in which the duties and further engagement of members of the police in Kosovo were defined. The essence of the meeting was to continue execution of anti-terrorist actions aimed at suppressing terrorism in Kosovo ... " Now, do you recall General Lukic in this meeting talking about how he had just met with minister Stojiljkovic and with the chiefs of department meaning General Djordjevic and then also the chief of the state security department? Do you remember him talking about that in this 2 December 1998 MUP staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly I do. It was the only meeting I attended, and it was very important for us. It would have been unreasonable for me not to remember it. What you just read out is what I can see for myself. The suppression of terrorism in Kosovo at the time of these events -- well, that was no longer. As far as I know at that time -- well, not at that time, but for two or three months before that there had been no activities concerning suppression of terrorism in Kosovo. The great problem of the time is what we discussed after the reports were submitted by the officers, were terrorist attacks against units and the casualties we suffered in such attacks. It was agreed that fire should be returned proportionately in such occasions. There was a lot of arms smuggling and other things. That was the way I understood it. It was decided that we should adequately respond to the terrorist attacks carried out against field units. That was the goal of it. I don't know how Sainovic could say that. As far as I recall, he was the main person in charge of the mission that was there monitoring the situation in Kosovo. I don't understand how he could have said this. Secondly, I claim that there were no operations because I would have been in charge of establishing communications. That did not take place. As of September, or rather, October, it never happened again because I dismantled the equipment, and it was no longer at those features. This is my explanation, if you accept it. I have no other explanation. There were no anti-terrorist operations at that time, but there were terrorist attacks and lots of casualties among the policemen. If there are reports to that effect, you could check that against what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify one thing, I think the transcript missed the part of the question, so just to clarify the question: Was do you remember -- do you recall General Lukic saying in this MUP staff meeting that he had been to a meeting with the minister and the chiefs of department for the public security and the state security, public security, of course, being General Djordjevic? Sir, that was -- do you agree that that was the question that you heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. But I wasn't there at that meeting which was attended by General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Correct. That was a meeting in Belgrade. I'm just asking you about this MUP staff meeting. Now, sir, I would like to clarify one thing. You stated with authority that there was no -- there were no anti-terrorist operations after October. However, in light of the fact that you didn't participate in planning, wouldn't it be more accurate to say that there were no anti-terrorist actions for which you set up radio communications?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No one could approve an action like that because that would mean suicide for units which would be without radio communications in that situation in the field in Kosovo. So I can say that in the territory where each village was a fortress unto itself and to have policemen enter that village and to be without the support of communications, there would be no chance for anything like that. Simply that is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So you are not aware of any MUP actions in Podujevo or in Racak in 1999 or after October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that these were actions for which the activation of action channels was necessary. I did hear of Podujevo. This was during the war, maybe the 25th, 26th, 27th, I'm not sure about the date. It was at the beginning of the bombing campaign. This was a crime committed against innocent people in Podujevo. I did hear of that crime. I know there were victims who were children, women. In such a situation, even one victim of that kind is too much. I mean, this is really something that I do know that happened. I know that it took place, but as far as I know, it was no action. It was simply a crime. To do something like that is a crime, and this is how it was described in the press too. Unfortunately, I say again because of my own duties and the duties of everyone in the staff this passed, and in the course of those events there were many victims. There were people who were killed. Among them policemen, terrorists, those killed by NATO bombs, but let's say this was collateral damage, whatever you want to call it. But this particular thing is a crime. As for Racak, this is something quite different again. This was an anti-terrorist action of a smaller scale and communication systems were not required there. This was a small area. I think I said in the beginning that -- which were the situations in which such connections were activated. If we had some small area where radio, hand-held radios were within range, this would be okay. They could use regular channels and by using the regular channels meant that this was not something for which channel -- action channels were necessary. There were some actions where it was possible to have the whole of Kosovo within range and to have communication with the staff. I didn't really take part in things like that. Well, this was a small action, but it's not a small action per se. There were many casualties there, but it was an anti-terrorist action on a minor scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, just to be clear, when you spoke of Podujevo, you are speaking about something that happened during the NATO bombing, not any action that took place starting in December of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you stated in your testimony that you were familiar with the October Agreements with the OSCE; do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just acquainted. I was just familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Were you aware that the MUP had to reduce their numbers in Kosovo under that agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it did reduce the numbers, not that it should have reduced the numbers, and I know that because the units that were coming to Kosovo later required much less equipment from me than the ones who came before. This was definitely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: But is it your testimony that you are not aware that was one of the requirements of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do know about that, and I know about it just the same as I knew that the mission would be in the terrain that we would need to keep them in good regard, that we needed to co-operate with them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last two or three sentences of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. If we can be a little bit more focused on the answers, we can get through with you tonight possibly, sir. I think you answered the specific question. Were you aware that the MUP also had to return heavy weapons that they had? Yes or no, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that piece of information. This is outside of my duties. Not MUP, I don't know what sort of heavy equipment MUP had. Perhaps they did have something. I know that the army had such weapons. I'm just a technical person so anything else really is something that I know very little about, and I don't know what the distinction would be, the line of distinction between light and heavy weaponry. That is something that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm really asking you these questions, sir, just to see if you understood the effect, whether these agreements had a significant effect on MUP activities in Kosovo. Were you aware of that, that it affected MUP activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: You know, unfortunately with this agreement which was good and should have been realised and was realised to a good part by the MUP, actually had a result that anti-terrorist attacks were stepped up. We had many more problems in terms of terrorism than before the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, my particular question to you was whether these agreements affected the MUP in Kosovo. Did you understand that they affected the MUP's activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm trying to say but in a kind of reverse way. So the MUP for the most part respected everything. Well, let's talk about people, let's not talk about weapons --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, this is not my question to you. Let me move on to the next question which is, were you aware that it was General Djordjevic who negotiated for the MUP when these agreements were finalised with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am hearing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, there's also evidence in this case that General Djordjevic was actively involved in the summer offensive in Kosovo in 1998. And, in fact, General Djordjevic himself testified here, and he said at page 10031 of the transcript: "In 1998 when the situation was most difficult I was down there, meaning Kosovo, all the time." Now, sir, based on your own observations of General Djordjevic in Kosovo, does that comport with what you observed in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I saw Mr. Djordjevic, you know, there. I know that Mr. Djordjevic -- yes, I saw him in the field. I know that Mr. Djordjevic was in the staff too. I saw him at the staff as well. So I know that Mr. Djordjevic was sitting in the office where I installed a telephone that he would use. This was a town line, not a special line. He had access to the staff, he could enter the staff whenever he wanted. He could have, I don't know how to say, I mean, it's nothing disputable. Mr. Djordjevic spent the bulk of his time touring the units. Most of the time he spent also touring the secretariats. More or less his stay there was approximately like that. In the staff itself at the meetings, I don't know if he attending them. Well, I attended them seldom myself, but I did used to see him there. I was still kind of there, yes. I don't know exactly what to say to you about that. He was in Kosovo in the capacity that he was in there. As far as command and control, that was in General Lukic's hands. If General Lukic permitted him to do any command and control, that was up to General Lukic. That was a matter between the two of them, and that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could just look at one exhibit. P699. Just the first page of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we could just look at the top of this, sir. Do you see this is a dispatch from the MUP staff? It's incidents of the last 24 hours on 20th of April, 1999. And do you see at the top that this is addressed to both the minister and to General Djordjevic? I'm just asking at this point if you can see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that the dispatches that went up to the ministry, that those were addressed both to the minister and to General Djordjevic, that he also received these?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Well, this can be unclear to me because I know that in the earlier period it just went to Stojiljkovic, and what this here could possibly be that it possibly went to Djordjevic in the event that Stojiljkovic was absent, perhaps that could be the justification. I don't know what else it could be. Because if it was just for purposes of information and if it was sent to Mr. Djordjevic, then there would be enough reason to be sent to the other chiefs of administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: But this here could --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that you are not familiar with the content of these dispatches. So why are you saying now that you know General Djordjevic did not receive these at any time? Why would you know that? You've told us that you are not familiar with the content of these.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never informed or familiar with the content. Never. I was not interested in any of the dispatch contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, I would put to you that there are other exhibits which I will not go through now. I could, for the record, name P694, P698. I won't go through those just to save time, but these also are addressed to General Djordjevic. Is it your testimony you are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I really don't know anything about that. I have never seen them, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So I just would like to return to P57, the last page, and I don't even know that we need to go back to it, I think we can remember this is the June 16th, 1998 document from Minister Stojiljkovic. Point 3 says that the head of the staff shall report to the minister about his own actions and the actions of the staff, et cetera. Now, you testified, sir, that not only were you aware of this point 3, but you testified that you were aware in practice that this is how it happened; correct? That was your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. We have just gone through numerous things, all of these after June 16th, 1998, I will list them now, that General Djordjevic after June of 1998 was actively involved on the ground in the summer -- in that summer offensive in Kosovo. That he participated in numerous meetings of the MUP staff in 1998, 1999, meetings where you were not in attendance, that you were in attendance at a MUP staff meeting where General Lukic said he had gone to Belgrade and met with both the minister and General Djordjevic about the security situation in Kosovo and the MUP in Kosovo, and General Djordjevic was also in charge of negotiations for the MUP in October of 1998, another fact of which you were not aware. Sir, my question for you is: How do you have any knowledge or basis with your lack of knowledge about the activities of Mr. Djordjevic and what he was doing to say that this point number 3 in practice did take effect? You can't say that, can you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that Mr. Djordjevic did not take part in the planning of actions. We are talking about a period when he was there, before October. He did not participate in actions. Mr. Djordjevic for the most part was with the units. Mostly with the units. I know that for a fact, and the people -- on the basis of the people who were there and who were with him, this was something that was talked about. When he would come to a certain sector and visited the people who were there in the trenches, this was a major thing. So this was something that was talked about. I can say one thing, I'm under oath. I was at the staff when the telephone would ring and the minister would reply or actually, Mr. Djordjevic would answer the minister's call and then he would ask for Mr. Lukic next to him. So you could not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are details and he did not -- and for me as a clerk, this was something very strange. We were in the room, Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Lukic, and myself who was there for some reason or other.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The entire witness's answer was not interpreted because it was not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I see Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, you've got the picture. Yes. You may need to retrace your steps a bit. Good luck.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Let's break this down a little bit. First you just said that, "all I can say is Mr. Djordjevic did not take part in the planning of actions." Since you yourself didn't take part in the planning of actions, you don't know that, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But so when the action was being worked out at the time I was at the staff. I was at the staff. When the action is worked out, I get the plan first. I said that. So I am there and then I should whether Mr. Djordjevic was inside or not, whether he had gone in or had come out, and I didn't see him, and believe me, so the first person who would receive a document about the completion of a planned action was me. I think that this was -- this was definitely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You would receive a map, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. But I would receive the map inside. I would not receive it outside. I would receive it inside, and I would be given it by Mr. Mijatovic or some other colleague of his. He would explain to me what it was about, and I would go. Thus, this was so. We can twist it now this way or that way, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, the main question is, I just went through with you a series of things after June 16th, 1998, showing General Djordjevic being involved in Kosovo, participating in plans about Kosovo, negotiating on behalf of the MUP with regards to Kosovo, all after June 16th, 1998 when this document by the minister was signed. Many of those things you said you were not aware of. So my question to you is simply: Because of your lack of knowledge of Mr. Djordjevic's activities and doings, you can't really say whether he was or was not out of the loop? You yourself don't have that firsthand information; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is fair to say. I didn't say anything that I didn't know, but the things that I do know, that I'm sure of, that's what I did tell about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you've already testified that you were not around General Lukic all the time. You didn't go to all of the meetings with General Lukic that he went to, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't listen into his telephone calls, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you didn't review his telephone logs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So while you can tell us that he had a certain number of conversations with Minister Stojiljkovic, you certainly can't say who else he did or did not have conversations with at other times; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that he spoke with some other persons who were perhaps not that important, but as far as co-operation of this kind, and we are talking about situations that were delicate situations, these were conversations. I was on a couple of occasions, or three occasions there when the minister called. I picked up the phone because I was there to hold that telephone. When somebody else comes, they continue and I go off on my job, so that is the truth. It's also that's the truth that he spoke with the minister, meaning talked and referred or reported about the situation and the events in the field. It is true that always thus any event that happened as far as terrorist attacks and such-like was something that he had to inform him about first. That is certain. That is for sure like that. And now if somebody was on the other side instead of the minister, just like I was there sometimes instead of Lukic, we can say that perhaps some deputy minister was there, he could have conveyed everything to the minister, but the minister could not tell me what I should convey to Lukic in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking you is although you can say that you heard Lukic talking to the minister on several occasions, you can't tell us that Lukic never spoke to on the phone or communicated with in some other way someone else, such as General Djordjevic? You couldn't represent that, could you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not, of course I couldn't do that. Naturally I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you have testified that you weren't part of the planning operations, you weren't part of the preparation for operations, you didn't get reporting on operations afterwards, you weren't familiar with the content of MUP dispatches, and, in fact, that that didn't interest you. So my question to you was, is this: You've testified that there was no plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo. If there would have been such a plan, sir, it is not very likely that you would have known about it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as such important things that were happening, there had to have been some kind of staff meeting which would have to have been attended by all because what we are talking about now is a very serious matter. It could not have been at a staff meeting or something and to have reached me from somewhere and to have been talked about. If something like that did take place, I would have had to have been there at the staff because this was a very important thing. This could have been some kind of secret meeting, some secret agreement that we had to have known about, and to have been able to implement it, but I really don't know anything about it. Had this really been happening and we in the staff didn't know anything about it, then that would be quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, anti-terrorist operations were quite important; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: The most important at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you didn't participate in planning those; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't participate in the planning of those, in the implementation of the, let's say, military operations, but I did know what was going on in the field because I was there a number of times and in the process of setting up radio communications I could follow what was going on in the field as could the head of the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, your focus was on whether the radio communications were working; correct? Your focus, and, in fact, you've testified that you were not interested in combat operations and the strategy of actions, that was not of interest to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. But, as I said, I had to follow the functioning of the entire radio network. For example, if they couldn't hear each other, it was a problem I had to solve. If one was trying to call another who couldn't hear him, and of course, I could overhear their conversations, and it is only natural that some of it remained in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. But it's fair to say that you were not aware of all of the plans of combat actions of the MUP, and in light of that, if there would have been a plan to expel Albanians, it easily could have slipped by you; fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know of the existence of such a plan, but I do know that an enormous amount of people during the bombings left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I truly know that. Great many of them. Especially in the Drim valley towards Kacanik and Macedonia. Also there were many going towards Bujanovci and Presevo. There were other inhabitants, Serbs, Roma, who left the territory of Kosovo. At the time, it wasn't very popular for officers to take their families out of Kosovo, but civilians were fleeing en masse. It wasn't easy to be there as bombs fell and refugee columns were struck. We can only discuss expulsions in that context. This is how I see it. And amidst all that are for someone to organise an operation to expel anyone, well, it wasn't necessary. People started fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honours. Those are all the questions that I have for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Petersen. Mr. Popovic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, in your testimony you said you attended one meeting of the MUP staff in its extended composition. However, as for the inner staff meetings, how many such meetings did you have occasion to attend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many more such meetings. Many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During those meetings of the inner staff, could you have drawn any conclusions about the functioning of the MUP staff in Pristina and the way operations were planned and prepared?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: At those meetings, it was mainly tasks that were issued. For example, communications tasks to me, and the situation and the staff itself was discussed for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend asked you how you knew of the plans and operations that were implemented. I have this question of you: When you received maps based on which you were supposed to set up communication lines, what was shown there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: On those maps one could see the movements of the units which were to take part in that particular anti-terrorist operation. Where I set up communication lines, there were usually three, four, or up to six units involved. They were indicated in red or blue indicating their axes of movement, and one could conclude what the goal of that particular operation was by looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to General Djordjevic now. In 1998 when you saw him in the field and you said it was in Malisevo and Jablanica, if I'm not mistaken, to your knowledge did he have any command role in those operations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: General Djordjevic had no command role to play. He never used our radio lines. He was never in any of our lists of call-signs. In such a situation, he had to keep in touch with the staff. He was never on any radio lines or communications, however, with the staff. This is what I claim in full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that you saw General Djordjevic in the MUP staff in Pristina in 1998, did you see him issue any orders to anyone at the staff or in the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know. I don't know how he spent his time there. I don't know. I know that there were no staff meetings at which Mr. Djordjevic -- Mr. Djordjevic participated in terms of contributions or as the head of such meetings. There were no such things. Maybe he had some arrangements with Mr. Lukic, but at the meetings, the meetings of the inner staff, he was never in charge of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You started discussing a certain event when the minister called and Mr. Djordjevic picked up the phone. The interpreters were unable to put that in the transcript. Could you please repeat your description of that event.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: It seemed unusual that the minister called and that his answer was -- his phone call was answered by the chief of the sector. And that they did not speak following that, but that the minister simply asked to speak to the chief of the staff. And then they -- the chief of the sector simply gave the receiver to the head of the staff, and following that I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, you said you were present when Lukic called from the staff to report to the minister. Were you ever present when Mr. Lukic called Mr. Djordjevic from the staff premises?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I answered that question already, I believe, but I also said that it wasn't completely impossible that he did so. In any case, I did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P699.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, you were shown this document by my learned friend. Look at the heading of this document, please. What is its title?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Survey of incidents, events, and intelligence of security significance recorded in the period between 600 hours on 19 April to --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: 600 hours on 19 April to 600 hours on 20 April 1999. I'd like to assist you since we are running out of time. Please look at item 1, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: Attacks by NATO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cankovic, is there a subheading or a subtitle on this page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, what does item 2 say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Terrorist attacks."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the title of paragraph 3? Perhaps we can zoom in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Serious crimes committed."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page. Please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What does paragraph 4 say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Persons of Albanian and other ethnic communities fleeing from the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page in the Serbian, please, and I think this is the last page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What does paragraph 5 say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Other."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cankovic, in this survey of intelligence related events concerning that date, is there any mention of terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, this concludes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Popovic Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have very few questions, Mr. Cankovic. What was your rank in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a captain, and I was retired as one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And did you wear a uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I never wore a uniform because I always worked on such things which would quickly destroy my uniform or make it extremely dirty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified about a meeting of the Serbian government in Kosovo in 1999. When did this meeting with the government take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting was held on the 15th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us that you had the opportunity to go back to Belgrade with one of the planes with your equipment. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: You did not. That was a joke made by my colleagues. I was supposed to go to Belgrade on that day, and I did, to pick up the equipment, and I also had a free weekend. I was supposed to go the day before, but I stayed another day because the prime minister was supposed to arrive. As the chief of communications, I was supposed to be there in particular for security reasons. Once they went to attend the meeting, I headed towards Belgrade in a vehicle. My work-mates jokingly said that I could join the government on the plane back to Belgrade but, of course, I couldn't. I was supposed to bring all the equipment along. Had it not been for that, I may have been on that plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, I missed obviously the word "jokingly." Do you know where Mr. Djordjevic went after the meeting of the government with the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I actually can't say. Perhaps around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m., I headed towards Belgrade. I had to leave the territory in daylight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell me where Mr. Djordjevic went after the meeting of the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't meeting concerning the prime minister. Yes, they went to attend the government session and then they had lunch together. That's what was planned. As for what truly happened later on, I really don't know. I don't know what the protocol was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You don't know where Mr. Djordjevic went after this event in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't really interested in where the prime minister was or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My last point, you qualified the event, the incident in Podujevo just as a crime and not as an action. Are you aware that there were at least two units of the SAJ were present just -- arrived just before the crime was committed and even more units of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: As for any units that were there, I could only have been aware of that if their commander would come in requesting some additional equipment or something of that sort. But as for my knowledge of any units entering or leaving, that is something I really had nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We've heard the evidence of one of the commanders of the SAJ, and he told us that he was given maps with a clear indication on which axis his unit should move. You are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I conclude from your answer that you are not aware of all orders issued in that way from the MUP staff by handing over marked maps to you to convey them to the units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: I never handed over maps to the units. I received maps that I was interested in, and these were usually excerpts, photocopies of topographic maps. But I never handed over any maps to anyone, not even as a mail person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know if the telephone communication from Podujevo, from the OUP Podujevo to Belgrade was working that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know whether the communication line in Podujevo was in operation that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That concludes the questions for you. Thank you for your attendance here and for the assistance you have been able to give, and you are now free to go back to your normal activities. When we rise, a Court Officer will assist you from the courtroom. The Chamber now adjourns until tomorrow at 2.15.
